round1_outcomes.CRIT-1_email_enumeration_429_oracle: CLOSED — handleUserNotFound now calls registerFailure(emailKey, ipKey) before throwing 401 (AuthService.java:130-135). Both wrong-password and user-not-found paths invoke the same registerFailure() helper that increments both keys, so the 429 threshold trips identically for existing and non-existent emails. Verified by AuthServiceTest::login_nonExistentEmail_runsDummyBcrypt_andIncrementsCounters_returns401.
round1_outcomes.CRIT-2_case_variant_bypass: CLOSED — login() canonicalizes via request.getEmail().trim().toLowerCase() at line 79 before any lookup or key derivation. userRepository.findByEmail and bruteEmailKey both receive the canonical form. AuthResponse/AppUserDetails consume user.getEmail() (the DB-stored value). Verified by AuthServiceTest::login_canonicalizesEmailToLowercase_forBruteForceKeyAndLookup. (Caveat: see new finding for Locale.ROOT.)
round1_outcomes.CRIT-3_sessions_password_hash_leak: CLOSED — AppUserDetails is now `record(String id, String email, String name, String status)`; no User entity reference. getPassword() returns null. UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.authenticated(principal, null, ...) passes null credentials. The serialized SPRING_SECURITY_CONTEXT in MongoDB sessions can no longer leak passwordHash, emailVerificationTokenHash, or passwordResetTokenHash. Verified by AuthServiceTest::login_success_invalidatesPreAuthSession_andSetsRememberMeTtl asserting principal.getPassword() is null.
round1_outcomes.CRIT-4_login_failed_events: OPEN (partial) — events written for user_not_found, wrong_password, blocked, deleted (4 of 5 originally listed paths). The brute-force pre-emptive rejection path (checkBruteForce throws 429 before user lookup) does NOT log a login_failed event with reason=brute_force. See finding BFE-1 below. Round 1 recommendation explicitly enumerated brute_force as a required reason — that path is the one most worth logging because it indicates an active attack.
round1_outcomes.MAJ-5_cookie_secure_default_false: DEFERRED-by-design — task description states 'kept dev-friendly defaults; production MUST set env vars; documented in decisions.md and Task 9 deployment.md'. Re-evaluated and downgraded to a minor finding/reminder (DEP-1 below) since the configuration knob exists and the decision is conscious. The risk is now operational (forgotten env var in prod), not a code defect.
round1_outcomes.MAJ-6_samesite_default_lax: DEFERRED-by-design — same rationale as MAJ-5; folded into DEP-1.
round1_outcomes.MAJ-7_xff_trusted_unconditionally: DEFERRED-by-design — code comment at lines 238-240 explicitly states the trust assumption and the production requirement (front with reverse proxy that overwrites the header). The behaviour is unchanged but the design choice is now documented inline. Downgraded to minor (XFF-1) — the unconditional trust still bypasses per-IP threshold if the deployment is misconfigured.
round1_outcomes.MAJ-8_timing_leak_extra_redis_hops: CLOSED — both failure paths now run identical I/O: dummy/real bcrypt + registerFailure() (which is two incrementWithTtl calls, each conditionally calling expire). The number of Redis round-trips and ordering is identical between handleUserNotFound and the wrong-password branch. Statistical timing oracle eliminated within Redis-latency variance.
round1_outcomes.MAJ-9_incr_expire_atomicity: DEFERRED-by-design — code comment at lines 165-167 acknowledges the small race window between INCR and EXPIRE under crash/connection drop and accepts the long-tail risk (Redis maxmemory policy bounds it). Lua not introduced. Re-evaluating: the impact (permanent counter without TTL, indefinite 429 for a targeted user until manual cleanup) is real but extremely low-frequency in practice (requires a Redis connection drop in the millisecond window between two pipelined commands). Downgrading to minor (TTL-1) for tracking and recommending a follow-up Lua script in the auth hardening epic.
round1_outcomes.MIN_useragent_storage: CLOSED — capUserAgent() at line 233-236 truncates User-Agent to 500 chars before storage.
round1_outcomes.MIN_getPassword_empty_string: CLOSED — AppUserDetails.getPassword() now returns null with explanatory comment (AppUserDetails.java:24-28).

findings.category: OWASP A09: Security Logging and Monitoring
findings.title: Brute-force 429 path is silent — no audit event logged when threshold trips
findings.description:
checkBruteForce() (AuthService.java:102-116) returns Mono.error(AppException.tooManyRequests(...)) when either threshold is reached, BEFORE userRepository.findByEmail() runs. There is no eventService.logEvent call on this branch. The 429 trip is precisely the moment a security operator most needs to see an event: it indicates an attacker has reached the rate-limit and is being throttled. user-spec line 80 lists login_failed as a required event type; round-1 recommendation explicitly listed `Map.of("reason", "brute_force")` as one of the five required failure reasons. Round-1 fix added events to four of the five enumerated paths but missed this one.

Operational impact: Brute-force attacks become invisible in events collection — the events show login_failed with reason=wrong_password or user_not_found up to the threshold, then go silent. SOC dashboards keyed on "events showing repeated failures from same IP" will UNDERCOUNT the actual attack volume because every attempt above threshold is dropped on the floor with no audit trail.

This is the same audit-trail gap that round-1 CRIT-4 was opened against, just for a different code path. Closing it requires a single eventService.logEvent call inside the .flatMap branch where the threshold check fails.
findings.impact: Active brute-force / credential-stuffing attacks are silenced in the events collection once they breach the rate-limit. SOC alerting and breach-timeline reconstruction lose data. Fails user-spec acceptance criterion for login_failed audit events.

findings.title: toLowerCase() uses default Locale — Turkish locale produces dotless-i variant bypass
findings.description:
AuthService.java:79 calls `request.getEmail().trim().toLowerCase()` without a Locale argument. This uses the default JVM locale. On a Turkish-locale JVM, `"USER@TEST.COM".toLowerCase()` returns `"user@test.com"` BUT `"İ".toLowerCase()` returns `"i"` (with combining dot above) and `"I".toLowerCase()` returns `"ı"` (dotless). For an email like `"İlon@test.com"` (a perfectly valid character in Turkish names), the canonical form depends on where the JVM is hosted. A user registered with `"ilon@test.com"` (regular ascii i) will not match a login with `"İlon@test.com"` if the JVM locale flips at restart, and the brute-force key on the lookup side will differ.

More practically: an attacker can probe variants in different unicode case-folding paths by leveraging the Turkic-i edge case. Even on en_US JVMs this is a latent correctness bug that bites the moment containers move regions or k8s sets LANG.

Fix is one Locale.ROOT argument. This is exactly the kind of bug that destroys CRIT-2's case-bypass fix in a way that's invisible in unit tests because tests run on the dev's locale.
findings.impact: Locale-dependent canonicalization can re-open the case-variant brute-force bypass (CRIT-2 round-1 finding) on certain JVMs/regions. Also breaks login for users with Turkish-locale-affected characters in their email local-part if the JVM locale changes between registration and login.

findings.title: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE / SAME_SITE defaults remain dev-friendly (false / lax) — production deploy depends on env vars
findings.description:
application.properties:15-16 still default to `false` / `lax`. Round 1 recommended flipping the defaults to `true`/`strict` with a dev-profile override. The team chose to defer this to deployment.md (Task 9) and rely on production env-var configuration. Re-evaluating: the trade-off is acceptable IF and ONLY IF (a) deployment.md explicitly mandates SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=true and SESSION_COOKIE_SAME_SITE=strict for production; (b) a CI lint/precheck verifies the env vars are present before promoting to prod; (c) decisions.md captures the deferral rationale.

The risk is purely operational now: a deploy that forgets to set the env var ships an insecure cookie. There is no defence-in-depth code-side check (e.g., a startup-time assertion that secure=true when SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod). One forgotten env var → session-hijacking-over-HTTP exposure across the entire user base.
findings.impact: Operational footgun. Single forgotten env var on a prod deploy → all users vulnerable to session theft via MITM or HTTP downgrade.
findings.recommendation: At minimum, ensure decisions.md and deployment.md (Task 9) MUST capture: (1) the env var values required for prod; (2) a startup assertion or CI check that verifies them. A defence-in-depth option: add to a @Component @PostConstruct that fails startup if SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE contains 'prod' AND server.reactive.session.cookie.secure=false. Or add a Spring profile-scoped application-prod.properties that sets `server.reactive.session.cookie.secure=true` and `same-site=strict` directly (no env var indirection). The latter is the cleanest belt-and-braces.

findings.title: X-Forwarded-For trusted unconditionally — documented but not gated by config
findings.description:
AuthService.java:238-240 now carries an explicit comment block explaining the trust assumption (production deployments must front the backend with a reverse proxy that overwrites X-Forwarded-For). Round 1 recommended a `app.security.trust-forwarded-headers` flag; the team chose documentation-only.

The documentation is clear and accurate. The remaining concern: a misconfigured ingress, an exposed NodePort, or any direct-traffic path defeats per-IP brute-force protection (threshold 20) entirely. Spring's ForwardedHeaderTransformer with a trusted-IP-range filter would be a stronger pattern. Downgraded from major because the design choice is now legible to operators reading the source.
findings.impact: Per-IP threshold can be bypassed by header forgery if the deployment lacks a trusted reverse proxy. Comment communicates the requirement; behaviour does not enforce it.
findings.recommendation: Track as a follow-up in a security-hardening backlog: introduce `@Value("${app.security.trust-forwarded-headers:false}")` and gate the XFF read on it. Add Spring's ForwardedHeaderTransformer wired only when the flag is true. Document in deployment.md and add a smoke test that without the flag, a forged X-Forwarded-For is ignored. Not blocking for Task 4 acceptance.

findings.title: INCR + EXPIRE atomicity race documented but not mitigated — long-tail counter-stuck DoS
findings.description:
AuthService.java:165-167 carries a comment acknowledging the race: between INCR and EXPIRE, a Redis connection drop can leave a TTL-less key. Subsequent failures keep INCR-ing without TTL ever being set. The user is then stuck at 429 until either: (a) someone manually DELs the key; or (b) the user successfully logs in (which DELs the key); or (c) Redis maxmemory eviction reaps it.

For a targeted user (no successful login because the attacker is the one trying), case (a) and (b) are unreachable. Case (c) depends on Redis configuration — the project does not document a maxmemory policy, so in dev/test this could persist indefinitely.

Severity downgraded from round-1 major because: (i) the race window is sub-millisecond; (ii) the impact requires both a Redis crash AND a targeted-account attack; (iii) the comment makes the trade-off legible. Still worth tracking — a 5-line Lua script eliminates the entire class of issue.
findings.impact: Edge-case permanent 429 lockout for users targeted during a Redis network blip. Hard to detect, hard to attribute, frustrating to support.
findings.recommendation:
Add a follow-up task in the auth-hardening epic to introduce a Lua script:

  local v = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
  if v == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
  return v

Wired through DefaultRedisScript<Long> on Spring Data Redis Reactive. Single round-trip, atomic, no race. Until then, ensure Redis maxmemory-policy is `volatile-ttl` or `allkeys-lru` so stuck counters eventually reap.

findings.category: OWASP A09: Security Logging and Monitoring
findings.title: login_failed events for blocked/deleted users distinguishable from user_not_found via reason metadata — minor enumeration leak through audit log
findings.description:
Round-1 fix introduced login_failed events with explicit `reason` metadata: `user_not_found`, `wrong_password`, `blocked`, `deleted`. The events collection now contains a higher-fidelity audit trail — which is the right outcome. However, an attacker with read access to the events collection (or any system that queries it) can use the `reason` field to distinguish:

- existing-but-blocked email (`reason=blocked`) vs non-existent email (`reason=user_not_found`)
- existing-but-deleted email (`reason=deleted`) vs non-existent email (`reason=user_not_found`)

This is an out-of-band enumeration channel: the HTTP responses are identical (both 401 for user_not_found and deleted; 403 with support email for blocked) — but the events row reveals the truth. Threat model: insider (support staff with read access to events) or an attacker who breaches the events collection separately. This is the same class of leak as round-1 CRIT-1's HTTP-status oracle, just shifted from the network to the database.

Not a HTTP-side enumeration vector. Acceptable for most threat models. Worth documenting because the events collection's access controls become a security boundary the moment this audit trail exists.
findings.impact: Insider/exfil scenario only: events collection content can confirm-or-deny existence of an email-bound account without distinguishing reason via HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Acceptable as-is given the audit-trail value. Document in decisions.md that events collection read access is a privilege boundary and must be limited to platform admin / SOC roles via MongoDB role-based access. Not a code change. Optionally, normalize the reason for unknown-account paths: `user_not_found` and `deleted` could share `reason=invalid_account` so reads of the events collection don't distinguish them — but this trades audit fidelity for enumeration resistance. Defer the trade-off to product/security review.

findings.title: DUMMY_HASH constant remains package-private — future-misuse risk persists
findings.description: DUMMY_HASH at AuthService.java:38 remains `static final String` with package-private visibility for AuthServiceTest reference. Round-1 minor finding unchanged. Risk is unchanged: a future contributor could write code that treats DUMMY_HASH as a valid credential check. Severity is still minor; this is a maintainability/anti-footgun concern, not an active vulnerability.
findings.impact: Future-misuse risk only. No active exploit.
findings.recommendation: Optional: rename to TIMING_PROBE_BCRYPT_HASH or NEVER_MATCH_HASH; add a SonarLint suppression comment; add a unit test asserting that the encoded password used to generate this hash is documented in a code comment. Not blocking.

verdict_summary: Round 1 closed 3 of 4 critical findings (CRIT-1, CRIT-2, CRIT-3) and 2 of 5 majors (MAJ-7 documented, MAJ-8 closed). One critical from round 1 (CRIT-4 login_failed events) is partially closed — 4 of 5 paths log the event, but the brute-force 429 path remains silent and is re-opened as BFE-1 (still critical because it is the highest-signal path for active attacks and was explicitly listed in round-1 recommendation). Three majors are deferred-by-design with acknowledgement comments and downgraded to minors. One new finding (Locale.ROOT) is introduced as major — it is a latent re-opener of CRIT-2's case-variant bypass on Turkish-locale JVMs. Two majors and three minors from round 1 are closed. Net: 1 critical OPEN, 1 major OPEN, 5 minors. Status remains changes_required pending the brute-force event log fix and the Locale.ROOT correctness fix.
